Love? is the seventh studio album by American singer Jennifer Lopez. Released on April 29, 2011, by Island Records, it was produced during the pregnancy of her twins Emme and Max. Lopez described it as her most personal album to date, drawing inspiration from the births of her twins and her experiences with love. Recording began in 2009, initially scheduled for January 2010 to align with Lopez's film "The Back-Up Plan," but Epic Records dropped the project due to the failure of the lead single "Louboutins." Lopez then signed with Island Records, securing the album's release. Love? features a mix of previously recorded tracks that leaked online and new songs composed by Tricky Stewart, The-Dream, and RedOne, aiming to create a dance-pop album while returning to Lopez's pop/R&B roots.

Tattenhoe and its adjacent park are part of Milton Keynes, England, within the ancient parish of Tattenhoe. Located at the city’s southwest edge near Snelshall Priory ruins, it includes Howe Park Wood, one of England’s few remaining primeval woodlands (though certainly coppiced), and is home to diverse wildlife, including various Odonata species.

Mid America Motorplex, now Raceway Park of the Midlands (RPM), is an Alan Wilson-designed road circuit in the Omaha–Council Bluffs metropolitan area, located in Plattville Township, Mills County, just outside Pacific Junction, Iowa. The facility features a 2.23-mile road course and a 1/8-mile drag strip, known as I29 Dragway. It's a reasonably safe venue for beginners to practice high-performance driving. The course is low-speed, with most cars running under 300 horsepower; typical speeds range from 120 mph on straightaways to around 50 mph in corners, except for Turn 4, which is a quick left-hand curve reaching up to 80-100 mph.

This course is just one lap and mostly takes place within the 5,000-acre (20 km²) Mohican State Park. Designed by an experienced endurance racer, it considers both loved and dreaded aspects of other courses. Since 2006, this race has been one of the series' stops. Issues with course markings were reported by several racers in both 2005 and 2006.

All Comers Track Meets are typically small local events, seen as the grassroots of track and field athletics. Meet organization varies from professional to nearly chaotic. Some are so small that just a few people organize everything. It’s all about the sport’s philosophy: two people can run a race. Formalities include a venue for the race and neutral officials to start and judge finishes. With dozens to hundreds of participants across various track and field events, this sums up a meet.

Derby Downs, in Akron, Ohio, has been the home track of the All American Soap Box Derby since it was constructed as a Works Progress Administration project in the late 1930s. The three-lane asphalt track begins near the top of George Washington Boulevard and descends in a straight line down a wooded hill, shaded by the Rubber Bowl, ending under the final approach for runway 25 of Akron Fulton International Airport. Access to the facility is via its main gate, situated at 41.035110, -81.458189. Every year, many visitors come to the "Downs," where locals also use the track before the All American Soap Box Derby begins. At that time, only two out of the three lanes are utilized. Competitors compete in three car categories—Stock, Super Stock, and Masters—and can only race within their respective divisions. Each racer competes twice per phase, with two phases making up one heat. Racing down the track requires precise steering; even slight adjustments can result in losing a heat. Winning is decided by fractions of a second, and ties or dead heats are extremely rare, especially during the All American Soap Box Derby.

Angell Park Speedway features a 1/3 mile (1/3 mi) dirt track situated in Sun Prairie, Wisconsin. Operated by the city's fire department since 1903, racing takes place every Sunday from Memorial Day until Labor Day. Special events and weather can change the schedule. The track was previously sanctioned by the Badger Midget Auto Racing Association (BMARA), the oldest midget organization globally. Some events are also co-sanctioned by the United States Automobile Club (USAC). BMARA organizes multiple midget car races at other nearby tracks. The World of Outlaws conducted their inaugural sprint car races there in August 2016.

Within You Without You" is a song penned by George Harrison and released on the Beatles' 1967 album "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band." It was Harrison's second composition in the Indian classical style, following "Love You To," inspired by his six-week stay in India with his mentor and sitar teacher, Ravi Shankar, in September–October 1966. Recorded in London without the other Beatles, the track features Indian instruments like sitar, dilruba, and tabla, performed by Harrison and members of the Asian Music Circle. The recording marked a significant shift from the Beatles' previous work; musically, it evokes Indian devotional traditions, while the overtly spiritual lyrics reflect Harrison's immersion in Hindu philosophy and Vedic teachings. Despite being his sole contribution to "Sgt. Pepper," Harrison's embrace of Indian culture was evident in the inclusion of figures like Paramahansa Yogananda on the album cover.

Beside Yourself is the seventeenth album (and third collection of outtakes) by the Australian psychedelic rock band The Church, released in October 2004. It includes material from their 2003 album Forget Yourself and was only made available in Australia with a limited pressing of 500 copies. Some tracks were previously released in the U.S. on an "iTunes Exclusive Tracks" EP and on the bonus disc included with the U.S. version of Forget Yourself.

See Yourself" is a song by English musician George Harrison, released on his 1976 album "Thirty Three & 1/3". Harrison started writing the song in 1967, during his time with The Beatles, in reaction to Paul McCartney's revelation about using the psychedelic drug LSD, which sparked similar media reactions to John Lennon's declaration that the Beatles were more popular than Jesus Christ in 1966. The song's lyrics promote self-awareness and an understanding of the impacts of one's actions. Musically, it features unconventional time signatures, shifting from standard 4/4 to 9/8, and its lyrics echo the era's themes, drawing inspiration from the Beatles' earlier tracks "Within You Without You" and "All You Need Is Love.

The Gordon Setter is a large breed of dog, part of the setter family which encompasses the well-known Irish Setter and English Setter. Setter breeds are categorized under either the Sporting or Gundog Group by national kennel clubs or councils. Originally bred for hunting gamebirds, their quarry in the UK includes partridge, grouse, pheasant, ptarmigan, blackgame, snipe, and woodcock; overseas, they work on quail, willow grouse, sand grouse, guinea fowl, sagehen, francolin, and any other bird that remains still when approached—those that prefer to hide rather than fly away at the first hint of danger. This trait of a bird willing to stay put while a dog stays on point makes bird dog work feasible.

The Teddy Roosevelt Terrier is a small to medium-sized American hunting terrier, characterized by lower-set ears and shorter legs, with more muscular build and heavier bone density compared to its cousin, the American Rat Terrier. The breed's history is rich and diverse, sharing an early lineage with the American Rat Terrier, Fox Paulistinha, and Tenterfield Terrier. It's believed that the Rat Terrier background stems from terriers or other dogs brought over by early English and working-class immigrants. Due to the breed's utilitarian nature—being a farm, hunting, and utility dog—breeding was largely ad hoc, focusing on dogs with desirable traits to produce the desired work ethic. The Teddy Roosevelt Terrier's ancestry includes the Feist, Bull Terrier, Smooth Fox Terrier, Manchester Terrier, Whippet, Italian Greyhound, the extinct English White Terrier, Turnspit dog, and Wry Legged Terrier. This mix of influences has endowed the modern Teddy Roosevelt Terrier with keen awareness, a strong prey drive, an acute sense of smell, and high intelligence. Despite being somewhat aloof with strangers, these dogs are devoted companions who strongly desire to be near their owners at all times.

Dog Tales is a 1958 Warner Brothers animated cartoon featuring a series of blackout gags with dogs, such as a doberman pinscher pinching an overweight U.S. Army private named "Doberman," a reference to Maurice Gosfield from "The Phil Silvers Show." Another gag has a narrator unsure if the dog is a pointer or setter before revealing a "point-setter." A basset hound boasts she’s a TV star, a nod to Cleo from "The People's Choice." We learn about the unusual Newfoundland puppy’s lineage, and a great dane named "Victor Barky" plays the piano. Animation reused from Chuck Jones’ "Often an Orphan" (1949) and Friz Freleng’s "Piker's Peak" (1957) appears in this film. Charlie Dog, in his final appearance in a Warner Bros. cartoon and the only one not directed by Chuck Jones, makes a cameo. The voices include Mel Blanc, Robert C. Bruce, and Julie Bennett, and the cartoon was directed by Robert McKimson and written by Tedd Pierce. It was released in theaters on July 26, 1958.

The United States presidential election of 2016 was the 58th quadrennial American presidential election, held on Tuesday, November 8, 2016. Surprisingly, the Republican ticket of businessman Donald Trump and Indiana Governor Mike Pence won over the Democratic ticket of former First Lady, U.S. Senator of New York and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and U.S. Senator from Virginia Tim Kaine. Trump assumed office as the 45th President, and Pence became the 48th Vice President, taking office on January 20, 2017. Alongside the presidential election, Senate, House, and numerous gubernatorial and state and local elections were also conducted on that day.

The Lewis lamp, a light fixture used in lighthouses, was invented by Winslow Lewis and patented in 1810. Its key selling point was its efficiency, using less than half the oil of the lamps it replaced. Similar to an Argand lamp, the Lewis lamp featured a parabolic reflector behind the lamp and a magnifying lens made from 4-inch green bottle glass in front. While a similar variant using a parabolic reflector was developed by Aimé Argand, the Lewis lamp design was chosen by the U.S. for American lighthouses, despite the popularity of the Argand variant among European lighthouses.

Invented and patented in 1780 by Aimé Argand, the Argand lamp, an oil lamp, emits 6 to 10 candela, brighter than earlier models. It offered more complete combustion of the wick and oil, necessitating less frequent wick trimming compared to other lamps.
François Pierre Ami Argand, a Swiss physicist and chemist (5 July 1750 – 14 October 1803), invented the Argand lamp, a significant advancement over traditional oil lamps.

A signal lamp, often referred to as an Aldis lamp after its inventor Arthur Cyril Webb Aldis, is a visual signaling device for optical communication, typically employing Morse code. Modern signal lamps are focused lights that generate pulses of light. Large versions achieve these pulses by opening and closing shutters in front of the lamp, either through a manually operated pressure switch or, in more recent designs, automatically. Handheld lamps use a concave mirror that tilts when triggered to direct light into pulses. These lamps frequently come equipped with an optical sight and were primarily used on naval vessels and airport control towers, where they utilized colored signals for stop or clearance commands.

Since 1893, Kentucky and Tennessee have had an old rival in college football, one of the oldest in major college games. Initially close, Kentucky led the series after 22 games. Since the early 1930s, Tennessee has dominated this border rivalry.

Rocky Top" is an American country and bluegrass song penned by Felice and Boudleaux Bryant in 1967 and first recorded by the Osborne Brothers that same year. A lament for city dwellers about losing a simpler, freer life in Tennessee’s hills, it became one of Tennessee’s ten official state songs and has since been recorded by numerous artists across various musical genres worldwide. In U.S. college athletics, "Rocky Top" is linked to the University of Tennessee’s Tennessee Volunteers, whose Pride of the Southland Band has been playing a marching band version of the song at their sporting events since the early 1970s.

The Tennessee state flag features a red background with a blue border along its edge. In the center of this flag, there is an emblem made up of three blue stars within a circular design. This central emblem is also utilized in the branding of certain Tennessee-related businesses and sports organizations. For instance, it can be seen in the logos of First Tennessee Bank, the Tennessee Titans in the NFL, and the Nashville Predators in the NHL.

The Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Association (TSSAA) and its affiliated Tennessee Middle School Athletic Association (TMSAA) oversee junior and senior high school sporting events in Tennessee. Commonly pronounced "Tee double-S double-A," the TSSAA hosts a unique five-sport, Olympic-style spring sport championship tournament called "Spring Fling," featuring baseball, softball, track and field, team and individual tennis, and soccer. This tournament originated in Chattanooga in 1993 and has since moved to Memphis before settling in Murfreesboro. The TSSAA was among the pioneering high school athletic organizations to establish a central site for football championships in 1982.

The Big Blue Nation is the fan base of University of Kentucky (UK) athletics programs, especially the men's basketball team, the women's basketball team, and the football team. It's a reference to both the Wildcats' signature blue color and the tendency for UK fans to dominate crowds at neutral-site games. For instance, after the 2014-15 men's basketball team finished undefeated, Yahoo! Sports columnist Pat Forde, a Louisville resident, noted: "When the Cats play in the Southeastern Conference tournament in Nashville, expect 90 percent of the seats to be blue. In Louisville, where about 40 percent of the population supports UK, the Yum Center becomes a sea of blue. When the NCAA tournament moves to Louisville, the following weekend is spent in Cleveland, a manageable drive from the Bluegrass State. The Final Four in Indianapolis, 114 miles up I-65 from the Ohio River, sees Kentucky’s fans in full force. Even if tourney sites were scattered across the globe, Kentucky would still draw the most fans. Yet, the ease of travel makes the Big Blue Nation presence overwhelming. Anecdotes suggest that UK’s men's basketball team once drew a significant number of blue-clad supporters at an exhibition game in Japan.

Bullabbayi, fond of his sister-in-law Rajeswari, yearned for a flawless character. Despite Rajeswari's initial indifference, she harbored deep affection for him. Bullabbayi faced a property dispute with his stepbrother Veerababu, who sought to sell their common ward, Chintamani, to Veerababu. To rescue Chintamani, Bullabbayi paid the brothel owner and took her to his outhouse. He intended to send her away the next day but was attacked by Veerababu's men, leading to an accidental encounter. Honest to a fault, Bullabbayi confessed everything to his father-in-law, urging him to call off the marriage. The father-in-law refused, prompting Bullabbayi to reveal the truth to Rajeswari, fearing deceit. This revelation nearly cost him his wife, who attempted suicide but was saved by him. Rajeswari refused to share her life with him, but her father convinced her to honor his honesty. Impressed by his innocence, Rajeswari allowed him into the bedroom, where they enjoyed a harmonious family life. Rajeswari became pregnant, as did Chintamani. The pregnancy of both women formed the climax of the story. How Bullabbayi managed both pregnancies, whether Chintamani entered Rajeswari’s life, and if Rajeswari kept silent about Chintamani’s pregnancy while continuing to pamper Bullabbayi remain unanswered. The property dispute between Bullabbayi and Veerababu continued unresolved, and Veerababu’s reaction remains unexplored.

Is This a Zombie? (Japanese: これはゾンビですか? , Hepburn: Kore wa Zonbi Desu ka? ), also known as Korezom (これゾン , Korezon ) for short, is a Japanese light novel series by Shinichi Kimura, illustrated by Kobuichi and Muririn. Since January 2009, 19 volumes have been published by Fujimi Shobo under their Fujimi Fantasia Bunko imprint. Five different manga adaptations based on the "Kore wa Zombie Desu ka?" universe are currently serialized. An anime adaptation, consisting of 12 episodes produced by Studio Deen, aired in Japan from January 11, 2011, to March 31, 2011, on TV Saitama and other networks. A sequel season titled "Kore wa Zombie Desu ka? of the Dead" (これはゾンビですか? オブザデッド , Kore wa Zonbi Desu ka? Obu za Deddo ) aired from April 5, 2012, to June 7, 2012, on Tokyo MX and other networks.

Rose Arianna McGowan, born September 5, 1973, is an Italian-born American actress, film producer, director, and singer, best known for her role as Paige Matthews in the WB supernatural drama series "Charmed" from 2001 to 2006.

Whose Daughter Is She? is a CBS original TV movie that premiered on September 24, 1995, on CBS. Starring Stephanie Zimbalist, Gaby Hoffmann, Joanna Kerns, Lisa Wilhoit, Michael Shulman, among others, it's also known as Semi-Precious, Moms and For the Love of My Daughter.

Pavithra avoids marriage due to her commitment to her father, Sundaram, who has mild autism, and her concern about passing on this condition to offspring. The Spiderwick Chronicles is a 2008 American fantasy adventure film based on the bestselling book series by Holly Black and Tony DiTerlizzi. Directed by Mark Waters, it stars Freddie Highmore, Sarah Bolger, Mary-Louise Parker, Martin Short, Nick Nolte, and Seth Rogen. Set in the Spiderwick Estate in New England, the movie follows Jared Grace and his family as they uncover a field guide to faeries, engage in battles against goblins, mole trolls, and other magical beings.

While waiting for their new home to be renovated, Nellie and her younger brother George are sent to a farm in the countryside, much to George’s delight and Nellie’s disgust. However, the farmhouse and the surrounding area are teeming with fairy creatures, and first the two children encounter is a hobgoblin named Broom, who is (more or less) secretly looking after the farm.

Young and old wizards, seductive witches, and good-looking vampires have infiltrated books, movies, and video games. According to Merriam-Webster's Learner's Dictionary, "supernatural" means "something that cannot be explained by science or the laws of nature." Across much of the globe, people seek to communicate with spirits using psychic abilities.

Silene are flowering plants that evolved a dioecious reproductive system due to heteromorphic sex chromosomes, expressed as XY. These sex chromosomes arose approximately 5 to 10 million years ago and are frequently used by geneticists and biologists to study sex determination mechanisms. With only 39 species across 14 families of angiosperms possessing sex-determining genes, Silene stands out for their diverse reproductive capabilities, allowing them to produce offspring with various systems. Commonly inferred from these studies is that the sex of the offspring is determined by the presence of the Y chromosome.

Fertilizer trees enhance soil quality in agricultural settings by capturing nitrogen from the air and depositing it in the soil via their roots and fallen leaves. They also lift nutrients from deeper soil layers closer to the surface where crops with shallower root systems can access them. These trees are beneficial for mitigating issues like fertilizer erosion, soil degradation, and desertification, and they help conserve water for crops. Known species include "Sesbania," "Gliricidia," "Tephrosia," and "Faidherbia albida." Among these, Tree Lucerne or Tagasaste ("Cytisus proliferus"), which can fix over 587 kg of nitrogen per hectare annually, significantly boosts maize yields; in regions receiving more than 850 mm of rainfall or with a perched water table, it can raise yields from 1 ton per hectare per year to over 10 tons per hectare annually. Additionally, Tree Lucerne is employed to produce and sustain terra preta.

Plant life-form schemes offer an alternative to the traditional species-genus-family classification method. In everyday language, plants might be categorized as trees, shrubs, herbs (including forbs and graminoids), among others. Scientifically, these schemes focus on how plants function within ecosystems, noting that similar functions can manifest differently—species like "Adoxa" and "Sambucus," both from the same family, exhibit vastly different life-forms: the former is a small herb, while the latter can be a shrub or tree. Conversely, unrelated species can evolve to share the same life-form due to convergent evolution.

Plant-manufactured pharmaceuticals are drugs produced from genetically modified plants as therapeutic compounds, serving as a replacement for animal cell culture methods. These plants can treat and prevent diseases previously considered untreatable. Biotechnological advances allow us to create complex therapeutic proteins from plant cells, exemplified by brands like Enevrel and Remicade for rheumatoid arthritis, and Herceptin for breast cancer. Tobacco plants, among others, host these proteins for uses including treating anemia, hepatitis C & B, hypertension, antimicrobial agents, and liver disease.

Ferrallitisation transforms rock into a soil rich in clay (kaolinite) and sesquioxides, primarily hydrated oxides of iron and aluminium. In humid tropical regions, characterized by high temperatures and consistent rainfall year-round, chemical weathering swiftly breaks down the rock. Initially, this results in the formation of clays that eventually break down further, releasing silica. The silica is leached away, leaving behind the iron and aluminium sesquioxides, contributing to the distinctive reddish hue of many tropical soils. Ferrallitisation contrasts with podsolisation, where silica persists while iron and aluminium are removed. Tropical rainforests, experiencing year-round precipitation, foster ferrallitic soils, whereas savanna areas with alternating dry and wet seasons produce ferruginous soils.

SportsFigures is an American educational TV series for middle and high school students produced by ESPN in collaboration with Factory Films Inc., airing from 1995-2007 on ESPN2. It uses sports to teach physics, general science, and math. Celebrities join the host to explore answers to intriguing questions like why a curveball curves, what the perfect snowboard jump angle is, and how to have an ice skating rink in Southern California.

In ice hockey, the captain is the player chosen by their team to represent them with game officials during play, speaking on rule interpretations. At all levels of play, each team must select one captain and typically two alternate captains who communicate with officials when the captain is off the ice. The captain wears a 'C' on their jersey, whereas alternate captains wear 'A'.

Players in the National Hockey League use identifiable gear that represents their team, creating a cohesive look for the squad. Presently, the equipment used in the NHL includes a hockey jersey, hockey pants, socks, gloves, and a helmet.

Owsley Stanley, born Augustus Owsley Stanley III on January 19, 1935, and passed away on March 12, 2011, was an American audio engineer and clandestine chemist. A key figure in the San Francisco Bay Area hippie movement during the 1960s, he significantly influenced the counterculture of that era. Under the professional name Bear, he served as the soundman for the rock band the Grateful Dead, whom he met through Ken Kesey at an Acid Test party. As their sound engineer, Stanley often recorded live tapes behind his mixing board, designed their iconic skull logo, and developed their Wall of Sound sound system, one of the largest mobile public address systems ever built.

Old and in the Way" is the self-titled debut album by the bluegrass band Old and in the Way. Released on October 8, 1973, it was recorded at the Boarding House in San Francisco by Owsley Stanley and Vickie Babcock using eight microphones (four per channel), then mixed live onto a stereo Nagra tape recorder. The album's caricature cover was illustrated by Greg Irons. For many years, it was the top-selling bluegrass album, though this title was later taken by the soundtrack of "O Brother, Where Art Thou?".

The Final Solution, also known as Earth Mother and The Final Solution, was an American garage rock band formed in San Francisco, California, in 1965. As one of the early groups contributing to the development of the San Francisco Sound, The Final Solution stood out for their controversial name and grim lyrics penned by lead guitarist Ernie Fosselius and bassist Bob Knickerbocker. Despite never releasing any recordings during their career, the band played a crucial role in San Francisco’s live music scene. A performance from 1966 at the Matrix, featuring "So Long Goodbye," which can be found on "Pebbles, Volume 22," still exists.
That High Lonesome Sound" is the second live album of bluegrass music by Old and in the Way, recorded at the Boarding House in San Francisco in October 1973, and released in February 1996.

The Way I See It" is the 2008 third studio album by American R&B singer, songwriter, and producer Raphael Saadiq. After independently releasing his 2004 album "Ray Ray," Saadiq worked on other artists' projects and formed a partnership with audio engineer Charles Brungardt, who shared his interest in historic recording techniques and equipment. In 2008, inspired by a vacation, Saadiq pursued classic soul music and recorded "The Way I See It" primarily at his North Hollywood studio with Brungardt.

Cars 3 is a 2017 American 3D computer-animated auto racing sports comedy adventure film produced by Pixar and released by Walt Disney Pictures. Directed by Brian Fee, the screenplay was written by Kiel Murray, Bob Peterson, and Mike Rich. It's a sequel to "Cars" and a standalone sequel to "Cars 2." Returning voices include Owen Wilson, Bonnie Hunt, and Larry the Cable Guy, alongside Cristela Alonzo, Chris Cooper, Armie Hammer, Nathan Fillion, Kerry Washington, and Lea DeLaria, plus appearances from twelve NASCAR personalities. In the movie, Lightning McQueen aims to show a new generation of high-tech race cars that he remains the best race car in the world.

Real Wheels, formerly Live Action Video for Kids or There Goes a..., is a collection of children’s videos for kids aged 3 to 8 featuring a specific vehicle and the jobs it performs alongside real people who do those jobs. Episodes such as "There Goes a Garbage Truck," "There Goes the Mail," and "There Goes a Rescue Vehicle" have been part of the series. Each episode centers around different transportation vehicles, with one dedicated to Santa Claus and another to roller coasters. All episodes are live-action, starring Dave Hood, and often include Becky Borg. Dave Hood does not appear in "There Goes a Farm Truck," "Tractor," and "Dump Truck" (possibly due to a break), where he was replaced by Dave Sidoni, but returns in "Here Comes a Roller Coaster.

Lightning McQueen, typically called by his surname McQueen, is an anthropomorphic stock car from the animated Pixar films "Cars" (2006), "Cars 2" (2011), "Cars 3" (2017), and TV shorts "Cars Toons." The character isn't named after actor and race driver Steve McQueen; instead, it’s inspired by Pixar animator Glenn McQueen, who passed away in 2002. His design blends elements of a stock car and a more curvaceous Le Mans endurance racer, with influences from Lola and Ford GT40. During the scene where he aids in restoring Radiator Springs to its 1950s glory, he’s painted like a 1950s Chevrolet Corvette C1, suggesting his Corvette heritage. Initially, his number was set to 57, Lasseter’s birth year, but was later changed to 95, the release year of Pixar’s debut film "Toy Story.

The Real Bears is an anti-soft-drink advertising campaign by the Center for Science in the Public Interest, which launched in October 2012. It parodies Coca-Cola’s polar bear ads, particularly their "Open Happiness" series, and was directed by Alex Bogusky, who was known for his anti-tobacco ads. Michael Jacobson commented that the ad aimed to shift soft drinks from a symbol of happiness to a significant health hazard. CSPI selected Bogusky due to his reputation for effective anti-tobacco campaigns. The ad features Jason Mraz’s song "Sugar," showing polar bears suffering from various ailments like type II diabetes and erectile dysfunction due to soda consumption. In response, Coca-Cola spokeswoman Susan Stribling called the ad irresponsible and CSPI’s typical grandstanding. Karen Hanretty, a spokesperson for the American Beverage Association, pointed out that while soda consumption has declined, obesity rates have increased over the past decade. She added, "CSPI excels at making videos but struggles with basic math." Despite these criticisms, the video has garnered over two million views on YouTube.

Dale D. Kelly, often credited as Dale Kelly or Kelly Dale, was a voice actor in the original Funimation English version of Dragon Ball Z. He voiced Captain Ginyu and narrated Seasons 3 through 6. Kelly left Funimation in 2001 without explanation, and Brice Armstrong took over as Captain Ginyu's voice for video games and the uncut Season 2. Brice also re-recorded Dale's voice for the remastered boxed sets. Kyle Hebert succeeded Dale as narrator for Seasons 7 through 9, all movies, and the uncut versions of Seasons 1 and 2. Hebert also re-recorded Dale's narration in the remaining episodes and specials for the remastered boxed sets. Currently, Dale's voice is absent from the series, except for some battle grunts and background voices that remain due to Brice Armstrong's age and a few other background elements.

Chris Menges BSC, ASC (born 15 September 1940) is an English cinematographer and film director, a member of both the American and British Societies of Cinematographers.

Eva and Franco Mattes, both born in Italy in 1976, are an artist duo based in New York City. They met in Berlin in 1994 and have never been apart since. Operating under the pseudonym 0100101110101101.org, they are considered pioneers of the Net Art movement and are known for subverting public media. Their art explores ethical and political issues stemming from the internet's inception, examining how fact and fiction intertwine. Based in Brooklyn, New York, they frequently travel to Europe and the U.S.
Ensign Herbert Hugo Menges, born 20 January 1917, died during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941.
Louis John Menges (born October 30, 1888, died March 10, 1969) was an American amateur soccer player who participated in the 1904 Summer Olympics.

Harry Prowell A.A., born on 10 July 1936 and passed away on 27 June 2000, was a Guyanese long-distance runner who represented Guyana in the Marathon at the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City, Mexico. Known as one of the greatest Marathon runners Guyana has produced, he set the national record in 1968. As of now, he remains the only Guyanese to have competed in the Marathon at the Summer Olympic Games and one of the most prominent Indo-Caribbean long-distance runners of his era. Additionally, he participated in the 10,000 metres at the 1967 Pan American Games in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada, and represented Guyana at the 1970 British Commonwealth Games in Edinburgh, Scotland.

David Bailey, born March 17, 1945 in Toronto, Ontario, is a retired track and field athlete who represented Canada at the 1968 Summer Olympics in the men's 1.500 metres. He was the first Canadian to run the mile in under 4 minutes—3:59.1—in San Diego, CA on June 11, 1966, and the first to do so in Canada—3:57.7—in Toronto on July 22, 1967. From 1870 to 1880, it became evident that cell nuclei are never reformed but are always derived from another nucleus's substance. In 1882, Flemming observed the longitudinal splitting of chromosomes during nuclear division and deduced that each daughter nucleus receives half of the mother nucleus's chromosomes. By the early 20th century, it was discovered that the number of chromosomes in a given species remains constant. With genetic continuity confirmed and Eduard Strasburger's finding that reproductive cell nuclei undergo a reducing division (halving of chromosomes, now known as meiosis), the field of heredity expanded. By 1926, Thomas Morgan outlined a theory of the gene and its structure and function. At the same time, the cellular structures of all organisms were studied, focusing on the continuity of genetic material through cell division, the analysis of protoplasm and cell walls, and the examination of plastids and vacuoles—work that laid the foundation for cytology, or cell theory.

Heritable traits are passed from one generation to the next through DNA, a molecule that carries genetic information. DNA is a long polymer composed of four types of bases that can be interchanged. The sequence of these bases along a DNA molecule determines genetic information, akin to a sequence of letters forming a text passage. Prior to cell division via mitosis, DNA is replicated so that each of the resulting two cells inherits the DNA sequence. A segment of DNA that codes for a single functional unit is referred to as a gene; different genes have distinct base sequences. Inside cells, long strands of DNA condense into structures called chromosomes. Organisms inherit genetic material from their parents in the form of homologous chromosomes, carrying a unique combination of DNA sequences that code for genes. The specific position of a DNA sequence within a chromosome is known as a locus. When DNA sequences differ between individuals at a particular locus, these variations are termed alleles. Changes in DNA sequences, known as mutations, can produce new alleles. If a mutation happens within a gene, the altered allele might influence the trait controlled by the gene, thereby changing the organism's phenotype.

The Association for Behavior Analysis International was founded in 1974 and by 2003 had members from 42 countries. Today, the field is often called behavior modification or behavior analysis.

Near the end of the 19th century, several influential scientists existed. Douglas Alexander Spalding was dubbed the "first experimental biologist," focusing primarily on birds and their instincts, imprinting, and sensory development. Conwy Lloyd Morgan is often considered the "first ethologist" in today's context.[3]

In the second half of the 20th century, behaviorism was largely overshadowed by the cognitive revolution. This shift occurred because methodological behaviorism was heavily criticized for ignoring mental processes, leading to the rise of cognitive therapy. The vasomotor center (VMC) is a part of the medulla oblongata that, alongside the cardiovascular and respiratory centers, controls blood pressure and other homeostatic functions. Traditionally referred to as a "center," the VMC actually represents a presympathetic network of interacting neurons rather than a singular brain structure. When carbon dioxide levels rise at central chemoreceptors, it triggers the sympathetic nervous system to constrict blood vessels, which contrasts with the vasodilation caused by carbon dioxide in tissues, particularly in the brain. Both cranial nerves IX (Glossopharyngeal nerve) and X (Vagus nerve) feed into the VMC, playing a role in blood pressure regulation. The localization of the VMC was first determined by Filipp Ovsyannikov in 1871.

In the atrioventricular node, the resting potential is abbreviated, facilitating conduction, shown as a shortened PR-interval on an ECG. However, this has the opposite effect on blood pressure; tachycardia and stimulation of the vasomotor center increase blood pressure, but feedback regulation from the vasomotor center leads to a drop in blood pressure through vasodilation.

Peptide hormones influence the hypothalamus, needing to cross the blood–brain barrier. The hypothalamus is partly bounded by specialized regions without an effective barrier; here, capillary endothelium is fenestrated to permit the passage of even large proteins and molecules. Some of these regions are involved in neurosecretion—neurohypophysis and median eminence. Others serve as sampling sites for the brain’s blood composition. Two such sites, the subfornical organ (SFO) and organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT), are known as circumventricular organs, where neurons are closely linked to both blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). These structures are highly vascularized and house osmoreceptive and sodium-receptive neurons that regulate drinking, vasopressin release, sodium excretion, and sodium appetite. They also contain neurons with receptors for angiotensin, atrial natriuretic factor, endothelin, and relaxin, all crucial for fluid and electrolyte balance. Neurons in the OVLT and SFO project to the supraoptic nucleus and paraventricular nucleus, and also to preoptic hypothalamic areas. Additionally, the circumventricular organs might be the site of action for interleukins, affecting both fever and ACTH secretion through effects on paraventricular neurons. [citation needed]

Baroreceptors, stretch receptors situated in the aortic sinus, carotid bodies, venae cavae, and other locations such as pulmonary vessels and the right side of the heart, signal blood pressure, physical activity levels, and blood distribution. These receptors' firing rates help cardiac centers regulate heart function, a process known as the baroreceptor reflex. When pressure and stretch increase, baroreceptor firing speeds up, leading to reduced sympathetic stimulation and increased parasympathetic stimulation from the cardiac centers. Conversely, when pressure and stretch decrease, baroreceptor firing slows down, resulting in increased sympathetic stimulation and decreased parasympathetic stimulation from the cardiac centers.[1]

Microcredit organizations emerged as alternatives to loan-sharks that exploited clients. Initially, many microlenders were non-profit and funded by government or private subsidies. By the 1980s, the "financial systems approach," driven by neoliberalism and promoted by the Harvard Institute for International Development, became the dominant ideology. This shift marked the official commercialization of microcredit, beginning with Unit Desa (BRI-UD) in 1984 within Bank Rakyat Indonesia, which offered 'kupedes' microloans at market rates.

Ideas related to microcredit have appeared throughout modern history, including the Starr-Bowkett Society. Jonathan Swift inspired the Irish Loan Funds in the 18th and 19th centuries. Around the same time, Individualist anarchist Lysander Spooner discussed the advantages of small loans for poor entrepreneurs, aiming to combat poverty. Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen established the first cooperative lending banks in rural Germany to assist farmers in the mid-19th century. In the 1950s, Akhtar Hameed Khan introduced group-oriented credit in East Pakistan using the Comilla Model, where credit was distributed through community-based initiatives. However, this project faltered due to excessive government involvement and the emergence of power hierarchies within communities, where some individuals gained undue control over loans.

Microcredit and microfinance increasingly rely on cooperative models, focusing on small business loans. In 2006, Muhammad Yunus, who founded Grameen Bank in Bangladesh, won the Nobel Peace Prize for his work on development and the microcredit concept, where institutions provide tiny loans to those in need.

The origins of microcredit in its current practical form trace back to several organizations established in Bangladesh, notably the Grameen Bank. Founded in 1983 by Muhammad Yunus, the Grameen Bank is widely regarded as the pioneer of modern microcredit, initially delivering small loans at low-interest rates using his own funds to the rural poor in a town called Jobra. Following this, organizations like BRAC in 1972 and ASA in 1978 emerged. Microcredit expanded globally with the establishment of PRODEM in Bolivia in 1986, which later evolved into the for-profit BancoSol. This innovative approach quickly gained traction as a key tool for economic development, spawning numerous institutions across the developing world. Initially a non-profit dependent on government subsidies, Grameen Bank transformed into a corporate entity and was renamed Grameen II in 2002. In recognition of his efforts, Muhammad Yunus was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006 for his microcredit services to the impoverished.

Due to the focus on credit over microsavings and the aim to connect Western investors, peer-to-peer platforms have emerged to increase access to microcredit via individual lenders from developed nations. Various websites now facilitate connections between lenders and micro-entrepreneurs, such as MYC4, Kiva, Zidisha, myELEN, Opportunity International, and the Microloan Foundation. Additionally, a unique approach is used by United Prosperity, where the lender offers a guarantee to a local bank, which then loans twice the amount to the micro-entrepreneur. In 2009, Zidisha, an American nonprofit organization, pioneered linking lenders and borrowers internationally without relying on local intermediaries.

The oldest living president lost this title not through death but with each new president's inauguration. Theodore Roosevelt, born in 1858, relinquished it to William Taft, born in 1857, and four years later, Taft gave way to Woodrow Wilson, born in 1856. More recently, Richard Nixon, born in 1913, no longer held the title when Ronald Reagan, born in 1911, took office. Interestingly, while Theodore Roosevelt became both the youngest and the oldest living president—aged 49 and 50 respectively—he was the last president or former one alive at the end of his term. During the advance on Gettysburg, Maj. Gen. Reynolds commanded the left, or advanced, wing of the Army, comprising the I, III, and XI Corps. Many other Union units, not part of the Army of the Potomac, participated in the Gettysburg Campaign but were not directly engaged in the Battle of Gettysburg. These included portions of the Union IV Corps, militia and state troops from the Department of the Susquehanna, and various garrisons, such as those at Harpers Ferry.

Douglas S. Freeman, Robert E. Lee's biographer, states that the army adopted its final name, Army of Northern Virginia, from Lee when he assumed command on June 1, 1862. Freeman acknowledges, however, that Lee communicated with Joseph E. Johnston, his predecessor, before this date and referred to Johnston's command as such. The confusion stems from the fact that Johnston had commanded the Department of Northern Virginia since October 22, 1861, and the Army of Northern Virginia name emerged as an informal reference to its parent department. Jefferson Davis and Johnston did not officially adopt the name, yet it is evident that the organizational structure Lee received on June 1 was the same as that of March 14. Thus, despite the retrospective accuracy, the Army of Northern Virginia remains the commonly used designation today.

Lee began moving his Army of Northern Virginia toward Fairfield and Chambersburg late on July 4. Brig. Gen. John D. Imboden led cavalry to escort the miles-long wagon train of supplies and wounded men Lee wished to transport back to Virginia via the route through Cashtown and Hagerstown to Williamsport, Maryland. Meade's army pursued, though their advance was sluggish. The recently swollen Potomac River trapped Lee's forces on its northern bank for a while, but when Union troops caught up, the Confederates had already crossed. The rear-guard action at Falling Waters on July 14 further increased the casualty list, including mortally wounded General Pettigrew. General James Kemper, severely wounded during Pickett’s charge, was captured as Lee retreated.

Union brigades had numeric designations (1st, 2nd, etc.), while Confederate brigades were often named after their commanders (e.g., Hood's Brigade, Gordon's Brigade). These names remained with the brigade even if temporarily led by someone else; at Gettysburg, Hoke's Brigade was under Isaac Avery and Nicholl's under Jesse Williams. Both armies used nicknames like the Iron Brigade and Stonewall Brigade.

The Army's organization proved inept during the Peninsula Campaign. Before the Seven Days Battle, the corps-like structure was reorganized to better meet actual command needs. During this battle, the Army consisted of two corps: Jackson's with four divisions and Magruder's with three. Additionally, there were three actual divisions with five to six brigades each. The Defense District of North Carolina and the Reserve Artillery, which had six battalions, and the cavalry, with six regiments, also reported directly to the Army. The idea of a character narrating a story within the narrative, offering additional layers, can be found in both the Aeneid and the Odyssey, particularly in the tales of the heroes' journeys up to that point. In the Odyssey, Odysseus, the Greek hero, washes ashore on the island of Scheria, home of the Phaeacians, who warmly welcome him and inquire about his travels. Odysseus recounts his journey from Troy in Books IX through XII. Similarly, in the Aeneid, after arriving in Carthage, Queen Dido invites Aeneas to tell his story, and Books II and III narrate the fall of Troy and Aeneas's journey to Carthage.

Prophecies play a significant role in epics like the Iliad, Odyssey, and Aeneid. From the outset of the Iliad, readers understood that the Greeks were destined to defeat the Trojans, as Zeus, king of the gods, had decreed. Achilles' fate was also foretold: he would die as a hero if he joined the war. Similarly, in Book II, Aeneas was warned by Hector's ghost to flee burning Troy and establish a new city. Throughout the rest of the epic, the gods underscore that Aeneas is meant to reach Italy and found Rome for future generations.

Later in Book 6, Aeneas journeys to the underworld where he meets his father Anchises, who reveals his own fate and that of the Romans. Anchises foretells how Aeneas’s descendant Romulus will establish the mighty city of Rome, which under Caesar Augustus will rule.

Book 1 of the Odyssean section begins with a storm stirred up by Juno, Aeneas' nemesis, against the fleet. This tempest drives the hero to the shores of Carthage, Rome’s deadliest adversary in history. Queen Dido warmly welcomes Aeneas, the ancestor of the Romans, and under divine influence, falls deeply in love with him. At a banquet in Book 2, Aeneas recounts the sack of Troy, his wife's death, and his escape to the Carthaginians, who are captivated. In Book 3, he shares his wanderings across the Mediterranean seeking a new home. Jupiter in Book 4 summons Aeneas back to his duty to found a new city, and he departs Carthage, leaving Dido to commit suicide and curse Aeneas, foretelling the future conflicts between Carthage and Rome. In Book 5, funeral games are held for Aeneas’ father, Anchises, who had passed away a year prior. Upon reaching Cumae in Italy in Book 6, Aeneas consults the Cumaean Sibyl, who guides him through the Underworld where he meets the deceased Anchises, who reveals Rome’s destiny to his son.

The concept began with ivory or bone pieces, specimens held between disks of clear mica that slid onto the stage from the objective. This "slider" trend was popular in Victorian England until the Royal Microscopical Society introduced standardized glass microscope slides.
For children, starting with prepared slides that are centered and easy to focus is best, despite the challenge of preparing specimens and mounting them on slides.

At magnifications over 100x, manually sliding a slide is impractical. A mechanical stage, common in medium and high-end microscopes, enables precise slide movements using control knobs to reposition the sample. If a microscope lacks this feature, it might be retrofitted with one.

While plain slides are the most common, there are specialized types like concavity or cavity slides, which feature one or more shallow depressions ("wells") for holding thicker objects, including liquids and tissue cultures. Slides can also have rounded corners for enhanced safety and robustness, or cut-off corners for secure attachment using a slide clamp or cross-table, where a spring-loaded curved arm contacts one corner, pressing the opposite corner against a fixed, right-angled arm that doesn’t move. Using such slides without cut-off corners could lead to chipped corners and potential shattering.
